cards.heading: Why private addresses
cards.body: There aren't enough public IPv4 addresses for every device. RFC 1918 reserves three ranges that anyone can use internally; they're never routed on the internet. To reach the internet, private addresses are translated to a public address with NAT (usually PAT).

cards.heading: The 172.16.0.0/12 trap
cards.body: Only 172.16.x.x to 172.31.x.x is private. 172.15.0.1 and 172.32.0.1 are public addresses.

cards.heading: Other special ranges
cards.body: 127.0.0.0/8 is loopback (the host itself). 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local (APIPA): a host gives itself one when DHCP fails. 100.64.0.0/10 is shared address space for carrier-grade NAT. These aren't RFC 1918 but aren't routed on the internet either. 100.64.0.0/10 is defined in RFC 6598. 192.168.0.0/16 contains 2^(24-16) = 256 /24 networks, from 192.168.0.0/24 to 192.168.255.0/24.
